cues.text: In 1429, at the Cathedral of St. Lawrence in Alkmaar, in the Netherlands, a newly ordained priest named Folkert was celebrating his very first Mass when, immediately after the consecration, he accidentally knocked over the chalice.
Consecrated wine spilled across the altar and onto his own chasuble, the outer vestment worn over his other garments.
Blood That Would Not Wash Away

The spilled wine, tradition holds, had become Blood at the moment of consecration, and no effort afterward could remove its traces from the stained chasuble — repeated attempts to wash the fabric clean left the marks exactly as they were.
The chasuble, carrying what the faithful took to be a permanent and inexplicable sign, was set aside for veneration rather than laundered again.
A distinct part of the wider Alkmaar tradition adds a further, later chapter.
A ship's captain in danger at sea reported an angel appearing to him, holding a cloth marked with three drops of blood.
The angel told him his vessel would be saved only if he sailed to Alkmaar and had the pastor of St. Lawrence unearth a buried cloth.
The captain did as instructed; the cloth was recovered and brought to the Bishop of Utrecht, who in 1433 formally recognized the event as a Eucharistic miracle.
An Angel to Hold the Relic
A statue in the shape of an angel was commissioned to hold the recovered relic, allowing the parishioners of St. Lawrence to venerate the stained cloth in a manner fitting its origin.

The relic and its angelic reliquary have remained associated with St. Lawrence Church in Alkmaar ever since, though the original church where the events took place no longer stands — the present-day St. Lawrence church is a later building.
The Alkmaar tradition spans a young priest's spilled chalice and a sailor's vision at sea.
It illustrates how a single local relic could accumulate more than one layer of devotional memory over time, each reinforcing the other's claim on the community's attention.
Whatever the precise historical relationship between the two episodes, the relic they left behind has drawn continuous veneration in Alkmaar for close to six centuries.
